claims.claim: The lithograph depicts the figure as it appears 'lying in state'
claims.quote: Views of right and left sides, as he appears lying in state.

claims.claim: The figure was about ten feet long
claims.quote: Whole length of the figure, 10 feet, 4½ inches

claims.claim: The lithograph 'The Onondaga Giant' is by Popular Graphic Arts
claims.quote: Title:  The  Onondaga giant ... Author: Popular Graphic Arts

claims.claim: The giant was dug up behind a barn on 16 October 1869
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: Two men were hired to dig a well and struck the figure instead
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant.

claims.claim: The giant.jpg image is a Bain News Service item dated 1910
claims.quote:
Date: 1910
Author: Bain News Service, publisher

claims.claim: The stone came from a quarry in Iowa
claims.quote: Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: The quarry was at Cardiff Glen, near Fort Dodge
claims.quote: VIEW IN CARDIFF GLEN. NEAR FORT DODGE.IOWA. This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: The quarrymen were told the block was for a Lincoln monument
claims.quote: telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York

claims.claim: The stereograph card names the culprits
claims.quote: Their names were George Hull and H. B. Martin.

claims.claim: The card was printed for locals who remembered the hoax
claims.quote: This is presented in remembrance of the generous response of Alonzo S. Weed A.M. to an appeal for aid for our Brethren and Churches rendered needy by the scourge of grasshoppers (or locusts) in the West in 1873—4.

claims.claim: The block went to Chicago, was carved there, then shipped east and buried
claims.quote: The block was taken to Chicago, the "Giant" carved, and then shipped to the point in New York which gave it its name, where it was buried in a barn lot, and subsequently "discovered".

claims.claim: The stereograph is dated 1873
claims.quote: Date: 1873

claims.claim: The giant has no hair because hair does not petrify
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: Hull consulted a geologist before carving
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified

claims.claim: The surface was beaten with knitting needles to fake skin pores
claims.quote: The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores.

claims.claim: Hull confessed
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: The barn belonged to William "Stub" Newell in Cardiff, New York
claims.quote: behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: Newell put a tent over the giant
claims.quote: He covered the giant with a tent and it soon became an attraction site.

claims.claim: Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute look
claims.quote: the next day, a tent was set up on the discovery site and Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant

claims.claim: Three to five hundred people came per day
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day

claims.claim: Cardiff's hotels and restaurants saw more custom in four days than ever before
claims.quote: The hotels and restaurants in Cardiff saw more customers in those four days than they had ever seen before.

claims.claim: The giant was carved from a gypsum block
claims.quote: hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: George Hull was a tobacconist
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull.

claims.claim: Hull lost an argument with a Methodist preacher about the giants in Genesis 6:4
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: In Chicago, sculptors Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann carved the giant
claims.quote: Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant.

claims.claim: The giant was shaped to Hull's own body
claims.quote: The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: The surface was washed in sulphuric acid
claims.quote: The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: Geologist John F. Boynton said it was not a fossil but guessed a 17th-century Jesuit carved it
claims.quote: John F. Boynton, the first geologist to examine the giant, declared that it could not be a fossilized man, but hypothesized that it was a statue that was carved by a French Jesuit in the 16th or 17th century in order to impress the local Native Americans

claims.claim: Andrew D. White of Cornell noticed there was no reason to dig a well there, the spot being convenient to neither house nor barn
claims.quote: that there was no reason why the farmer should dig a well in the spot where the figure was found; that it was convenient neither to the house nor to the barn

claims.claim: Yale's Othniel C. Marsh called it "a most decided humbug" and argued soluble gypsum buried for centuries would not keep fresh tool marks
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue, pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did), and termed it "a most decided humbug".

claims.claim: Hull confessed on December 10, 1869
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: Hull said he confessed proudly, to show how easily people believe
claims.quote: confessed proudly that he intended for the hoax to be exposed to reveal the tendency of the Christian community to believe in things too easily

claims.claim: It is unsettled whether Edward Burkhardt, the Chicago stonecutter, knew what he was making
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions, it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving

claims.claim: The copy in a Michigan arcade is only claimed to be Barnum's
claims.quote: The owner of Marvin's Marvelous Mechanical Museum, a coin-operated game arcade and museum of oddities in Farmington Hills, Michigan, has said that the copy displayed there is Barnum's.

claims.claim: The lithograph dates from 1869
claims.quote: Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1869, by A.L. Edwards in the Clerk's Office, of the District Court, for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.

claims.claim: The 1873 stereograph of Cardiff Glen comes from the New York Public Library
